question.text:
You are analyzing the performance of two mutual funds over the past decade: Fund X: Annualized Return = 8.5%, Standard Deviation = 12% Fund Y: Annualized Return = 9%, Standard Deviation = 10
Rank the funds based on risk-adjusted return using the Sharpe Ratio.

answer.text: Both funds have the same risk-adjusted return
Cannot determine from the given data

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe Ratio = (Return – Risk-free rate) / Standard Deviation. Using a 2% risk-free rate: Fund X = (8.5% – 2%) / 12% = 0.54; Fund Y = (9% – 2%) / 10% = 0.70. Fund Y delivers more return per unit of total risk, so Y ranks ahead of X. The Trap: Ranking X first looks at the raw return numbers and ignores risk. 'Same risk-adjusted return' ignores the 0.70 vs 0.54 gap. 'Cannot determine' is wrong because the risk-free rate is a standard assumption and both inputs are given. Cross-Exam Context: Sharpe Ratio appears in NISM XV, XXI-B (PMS Managers), XIX-C/D/E (AIF Managers) and V-A for risk-adjusted fund comparison. Distributor's Pro-Tip: When an HNI compares two PMS strategies quoting only CAGR, compute and show the Sharpe differential — it is the single cleanest way to justify a higher-fee, lower-volatility strategy over a hot-return rival.
